title: The psychology of “wrong time”: six biases
objectives: Name six biases from what the client says, and the response to each.
Explain loss aversion, hindsight and anchoring with client quotes.
body_md:
Regret: “I should have waited.” Response: acknowledge the feeling; shift focus to what can still be controlled. Hindsight bias: “It was obvious the market would fall.” Response: it only looks obvious afterwards; few predicted it beforehand. Loss aversion: “I just want my money back, then I'll exit.” Response: the decision should depend on the goal, not on breaking even. Recency bias: “Markets only go down now.” Response: show past falls and recoveries; nothing is guaranteed, but falls have historically been temporary for diversified equity. Anchoring: “I bought at ₹50; I'll sell when it's back to ₹50.” Response: the purchase price is irrelevant to whether the fund suits the goal today. Waiting for the perfect time: “I'll invest after the next dip.” Response: show the cost of waiting (Example 3).

| Bias | What the client says | How to respond |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regret | "I should have waited." | Acknowledge the feeling; shift focus to what can still be controlled |
| Hindsight bias | "It was obvious the market would fall." | It only looks obvious afterwards; few predicted it beforehand |
| Loss aversion | "I just want my money back, then I'll exit." | The decision should depend on the goal, not on breaking even |
| Recency bias | "Markets only go down now." | Show past falls and recoveries; nothing is guaranteed, but falls have historically been temporary for diversified equity |
| Anchoring | "I bought at ₹50; I'll sell when it's back to ₹50." | The purchase price is irrelevant to whether the fund suits the goal today |
| Waiting for the perfect time | "I'll invest after the next dip." | Show the cost of waiting (Example 3) |

> **Talk-track:** “Nobody can pick the perfect day. What we can control is staying invested for your goal, adding when prices are low, and not making a permanent decision in a temporary fall.”
example: “I bought at ₹50; I'll sell when it's back to ₹50”: anchoring — the purchase price doesn't decide whether the fund suits the goal today.
say: Decide by the goal, not by breaking even.
The purchase price is irrelevant to suitability today.
never: Dismiss the client's concern as irrational.
Agree that the fall was obvious in advance.

check.q: “I bought at ₹50, so I’ll sell when it’s back to ₹50” is an example of…
check.why: Anchoring. Fixing on a past price is anchoring.

check.q: “It was obvious the market would crash” reflects…
check.why: Hindsight bias. Events look predictable only after they happen.
